# Activity: Reading Derivatives from Graphs

<!-- ::: {.callout-note}
## About this activity
An in-class, pencil-and-paper worksheet. You will practice passing between the graph of a
function $f$ and the graph of its derivative $f'$ — in both directions. Going from $f$ to $f'$
always has a single answer; going from $f'$ back to $f$ does not, and finding out exactly how
much is missing is the main point of the second half.
Companion reading: C&J §2.8.a, §2.8.e–f, and §2.9.b.
::: -->

```{python}
#| echo: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

BLUE, RED, GRAY = "C0", "C3", "0.6"


def grid_axes(ax, xlim, ylim, title, ylabel="$y$"):
    xmin, xmax = xlim
    ymin, ymax = ylim
    ax.set_xticks(range(xmin, xmax + 1))
    ax.set_yticks(range(ymin, ymax + 1))
    ax.grid(True, color="0.85", lw=0.6)
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.25", lw=1.1)
    ax.axvline(0, color="0.25", lw=1.1)
    ax.set_xlim(xmin - 0.3, xmax + 0.3)
    ax.set_ylim(ymin - 0.3, ymax + 0.3)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax.set_title(title)
    for side in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)


def stacked(xlim, panels, width=6.5, unit=0.36):
    """Axes stacked vertically with a common x-range, so that x-positions line up.
    panels: list of (ylim, title, ylabel)."""
    heights = [p[0][1] - p[0][0] + 1.5 for p in panels]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        len(panels), 1,
        figsize=(width, unit * sum(heights) + 0.5 * len(panels)),
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": heights},
        layout="constrained",
    )
    for ax, (ylim, title, ylabel) in zip(axes, panels):
        grid_axes(ax, xlim, ylim, title, ylabel)
    return fig, axes


def curve(ax, f, a, b, color=BLUE, lw=2.2, **kw):
    x = np.linspace(a, b, 400)
    ax.plot(x, f(x), color=color, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="round", **kw)


def hole(ax, x, y, color=BLUE):
    ax.plot([x], [y], "o", ms=6, mfc="white", mec=color, mew=1.8, zorder=5)


def dot(ax, x, y, color=RED):
    ax.plot([x], [y], "o", ms=6, color=color, zorder=5)


def guides(axes, xs):
    for ax in axes:
        for x in xs:
            ax.axvline(x, color=GRAY, lw=1, ls="--", zorder=0)


# ---- Problem 1 ------------------------------------------------------------
f1 = lambda x: (x**3 - 12 * x) / 8
f1p = lambda x: 3 * (x**2 - 4) / 8

# ---- Problem 2 (corner at x = 1) ------------------------------------------
f2_left = lambda x: (x + 1) ** 3 / 4 + 1      # on [-3, 1]
f2_right = lambda x: 4 - x                    # on [1, 3]
f2p_left = lambda x: 3 * (x + 1) ** 2 / 4     # on [-3, 1)
f2p_right = lambda x: -1 + 0 * x              # on (1, 3]

# ---- Problem 3 (piecewise-linear derivative) -------------------------------
P3_pts = np.array([[-4, -2], [0, 2], [2, 2], [4, -2]])
def f3p(x):
    return np.interp(x, P3_pts[:, 0], P3_pts[:, 1])
def f3(x, c):                                  # c = f(0)
    x = np.asarray(x, float)
    return np.where(x <= 0, x**2 / 2 + 2 * x + c,
           np.where(x <= 2, 2 * x + c, -x**2 + 6 * x + c - 4))

# ---- Problem 4 (jump in the derivative at x = 0) ---------------------------
f4p_left = lambda x: x + 1                     # on [-3, 0)
f4p_right = lambda x: 3 * (x - 2) ** 2 / 4     # on (0, 3]
def f4(x, c):                                  # c = f(0)
    x = np.asarray(x, float)
    return np.where(x <= 0, x**2 / 2 + x + c, c + ((x - 2) ** 3 + 8) / 4)
```

## Background

For now we use the geometric meaning of the derivative: $f'(x_0)$ is the **slope of the tangent
line** to the graph of $f$ at the point $(x_0, f(x_0))$. Reading off a slope from a graph means
laying a ruler along the curve at $x_0$ and measuring rise over run, using the grid squares.
Doing this at every $x$ produces a new function, $x \mapsto f'(x)$, with its own graph.

## Warm-up: a dictionary

::: {#exr-deriv-dictionary}
Complete the right-hand column. Each row translates a feature of the graph of $f$ into a feature
of the graph of $f'$.

| If the graph of $f$ … | … then the graph of $f'$ … |
|:--|:--|
| is increasing on an interval | &nbsp; |
| is decreasing on an interval | &nbsp; |
| has a horizontal tangent at $x_0$ | &nbsp; |
| is a straight line of slope $m$ on an interval | &nbsp; |
| bends upward (is concave up) on an interval | &nbsp; |
| bends downward (is concave down) on an interval | &nbsp; |
| changes from bending down to bending up (inflection point) at $x_0$ | &nbsp; |
| has a corner at $x_0$ | &nbsp; |
:::

::: {.solution}
| If the graph of $f$ … | … then the graph of $f'$ … |
|:--|:--|
| is increasing on an interval | lies on or above the $x$-axis there |
| is decreasing on an interval | lies on or below the $x$-axis there |
| has a horizontal tangent at $x_0$ | meets the $x$-axis at $x_0$: $f'(x_0)=0$ |
| is a straight line of slope $m$ on an interval | is the horizontal line at height $m$ there |
| bends upward (is concave up) on an interval | is increasing there |
| bends downward (is concave down) on an interval | is decreasing there |
| changes from bending down to bending up at $x_0$ | has a local minimum at $x_0$ |
| has a corner at $x_0$ | has no value at $x_0$; it typically jumps there |

Note "on or above" in the first row, not "above": $x \mapsto x^3$ is strictly increasing,
yet its tangent at $0$ is horizontal. A zero of $f'$ does *not* by itself signal a maximum or
minimum. Problems 2 and 4 contain exactly this situation.
:::

## Part I: From $f$ to $f'$

In each problem, the top panel shows the graph of $f$. Sketch the graph of $f'$ on the empty
axes below it; the $x$-axes are aligned, so you can transfer $x$-coordinates straight down.

### Problem 1

```{python}
#| label: fig-deriv-p1
#| fig-cap: "Problem 1: the graph of $f$ (top) and axes for your sketch of $f'$ (bottom)."
#| echo: false
fig, (ax_f, ax_d) = stacked((-4, 4), [((-3, 3), "Graph of $f$", "$y$"),
                                      ((-2, 5), "Sketch the graph of $f'$ here", "$y$")])
curve(ax_f, f1, -4, 4)
plt.show()
```

::: {#exr-deriv-p1}
1.  Find all points where the tangent to $f$ is horizontal. Mark the corresponding zeros of $f'$
    on the lower axes.
2.  Between these points, decide whether $f$ is increasing or decreasing, and hence whether the
    graph of $f'$ lies above or below the $x$-axis.
3.  Where is $f$ *steepest* while going down? What does that tell you about $f'$ there?
4.  Estimate slopes with a ruler and fill in the table. Plot the points on the lower axes.

    | $x$ | $-4$ | $-3$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
    |:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
    | $f'(x)\approx$ | &nbsp; | &nbsp; | &nbsp; | &nbsp; | &nbsp; | &nbsp; | &nbsp; | &nbsp; | &nbsp; |

5.  Connect your points to a smooth sketch of $f'$. Check it against the dictionary: where $f$
    bends up, is your $f'$ increasing?
:::

::: {.solution}
The function is $f(x) = \tfrac18(x^3 - 12x)$, so $f'(x) = \tfrac38(x^2-4)$, an upward parabola.

```{python}
#| label: fig-deriv-p1-sol
#| fig-cap: "Solution to Problem 1."
#| echo: false
fig, (ax_f, ax_d) = stacked((-4, 4), [((-3, 3), "$f$", "$y$"), ((-2, 5), "$f'$", "$y$")])
curve(ax_f, f1, -4, 4)
curve(ax_d, f1p, -4, 4, color=RED)
for x0 in (-2, 0, 2):
    dot(ax_f, x0, f1(x0), color=BLUE); dot(ax_d, x0, f1p(x0))
guides((ax_f, ax_d), (-2, 0, 2))
plt.show()
```

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-3$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| $f'(x)$ | $4.5$ | $1.875$ | $0$ | $-1.125$ | $-1.5$ | $-1.125$ | $0$ | $1.875$ | $4.5$ |

- Horizontal tangents at $x=\pm2$ (local max at $-2$, local min at $2$), so $f'(\pm2)=0$.
- $f$ increases on $[-4,-2]$ and $[2,4]$ ($f'\ge 0$) and decreases on $[-2,2]$ ($f'\le 0$).
- The steepest descent is at the inflection point $x=0$, where $f'$ has its minimum $-1.5$.
- $f$ bends down on $[-4,0]$ and up on $[0,4]$, matching $f'$ decreasing, then increasing.
:::

### Problem 2

```{python}
#| label: fig-deriv-p2
#| fig-cap: "Problem 2: the graph of $f$ (top) and axes for your sketch of $f'$ (bottom)."
#| echo: false
fig, (ax_f, ax_d) = stacked((-3, 3), [((-2, 4), "Graph of $f$", "$y$"),
                                      ((-2, 4), "Sketch the graph of $f'$ here", "$y$")])
curve(ax_f, f2_left, -3, 1)
curve(ax_f, f2_right, 1, 3)
plt.show()
```

::: {#exr-deriv-p2}
1.  At $x=-1$ the tangent to $f$ is horizontal. Does $f$ have a maximum or a minimum there? What
    does the graph of $f'$ do near $x=-1$ — does it cross the $x$-axis or only touch it?
2.  To the right of $x=1$ the graph of $f$ is a straight line. What is its slope, and what does
    $f'$ look like there?
3.  What happens at $x = 1$? Compare the slopes just to the left and just to the right of $1$.
    Is there a sensible value for $f'(1)$? How do you show this in your sketch?
4.  Sketch $f'$ on the whole interval $[-3,3]$.
:::

::: {.solution}
On $[-3,1]$, $f(x) = \tfrac14(x+1)^3 + 1$, so $f'(x) = \tfrac34(x+1)^2$; on $[1,3]$,
$f(x) = 4-x$, so $f'(x) = -1$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-deriv-p2-sol
#| fig-cap: "Solution to Problem 2. The open circles mark that $f'(1)$ is undefined."
#| echo: false
fig, (ax_f, ax_d) = stacked((-3, 3), [((-2, 4), "$f$", "$y$"), ((-2, 4), "$f'$", "$y$")])
curve(ax_f, f2_left, -3, 1); curve(ax_f, f2_right, 1, 3)
curve(ax_d, f2p_left, -3, 1, color=RED); curve(ax_d, f2p_right, 1, 3, color=RED)
hole(ax_d, 1, 3, RED); hole(ax_d, 1, -1, RED)
dot(ax_f, -1, 1, color=BLUE); dot(ax_d, -1, 0)
guides((ax_f, ax_d), (-1, 1))
plt.show()
```

- At $x=-1$ the tangent is horizontal, yet $f$ keeps increasing on both sides: there is no
  extremum. Accordingly the graph of $f'$ **touches** the $x$-axis at $-1$ without crossing it.
  (A "flat" inflection point, as for $x^3$ at $0$.)
- On $(1,3]$ the graph is a line of slope $-1$, so $f'$ is constantly $-1$.
- Just left of $1$ the slope is close to $3$; just right of $1$ it is $-1$. No single tangent
  line fits at the corner, so $f'(1)$ is undefined, and the graph of $f'$ **jumps** from $3$ to
  $-1$. We draw open circles at both ends. Note that $f$ itself is continuous at $1$: continuity
  does not guarantee a derivative (C&J §2.8.e).
:::

## Part II: From $f'$ back to $f$

Now the roles are reversed: the top panel shows the graph of the **derivative** $f'$, and your
task is to sketch $f$ itself.

### Problem 3

```{python}
#| label: fig-deriv-p3
#| fig-cap: "Problem 3: the graph of $f'$ (top) and two sets of axes for your sketches of $f$."
#| echo: false
fig, (ax_d, ax_a, ax_b) = stacked((-4, 4), [((-3, 3), "Graph of $f'$", "$y$"),
                                             ((-2, 7), "Axes A: sketches for parts 2 and 3", "$y$"),
                                             ((-2, 7), "Axes B: sketch for part 5", "$y$")])
curve(ax_d, f3p, -4, 4)
plt.show()
```

::: {#exr-deriv-p3}
1.  Read off from the graph of $f'$: on which intervals is $f$ increasing or decreasing? Where
    does $f$ have a local maximum or minimum? Where does $f$ bend up, where does it bend down, and
    where is it a straight line (with what slope)?
2.  Sketch **a** function $f$ with this derivative on axes A.
3.  Compare your sketch with your neighbor's. Are they the same? On axes A, sketch a *second*
    function that also has the derivative shown, but is different from your first one. How are
    the two graphs related to each other?
4.  Describe all functions whose derivative is the one shown. How much information about $f$ is
    the graph of $f'$ missing?
5.  Now suppose you are also told that
    $$
    f(-2) = -1.
    $$
    Sketch $f$ on axes B. Is there now only one possible graph? Read off approximate values of
    $f(-4)$, $f(0)$, $f(2)$, $f(3)$, and $f(4)$ from your sketch.
:::

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| label: fig-deriv-p3-sol
#| fig-cap: "Solution to Problem 3. Gray: several functions with the given derivative. Red: the one with $f(-2) = -1$."
#| echo: false
fig, (ax_d, ax_s) = stacked((-4, 4), [((-3, 3), "$f'$", "$y$"), ((-3, 8), "$f$", "$y$")])
curve(ax_d, f3p, -4, 4)
for c in (-1, 0, 2, 3):
    curve(ax_s, lambda x, c=c: f3(x, c), -4, 4, color=GRAY, lw=1.3)
curve(ax_s, lambda x: f3(x, 1), -4, 4, color=RED)
dot(ax_s, -2, -1)
guides((ax_d, ax_s), (-2, 0, 2, 3))
plt.show()
```

1.  $f' < 0$ on $[-4,-2)$ and $(3,4]$, $f'>0$ on $(-2,3)$: $f$ decreases, then increases, then
    decreases, with a local minimum at $x=-2$ and a local maximum at $x=3$. Since $f'$ increases
    on $[-4,0]$, $f$ bends up there; on $[0,2]$, $f'=2$ is constant, so $f$ is a straight line
    of slope $2$; on $[2,4]$, $f'$ decreases, so $f$ bends down.
2.  A correct sketch has all the features from part 1; where it sits vertically is up to you.
3.  Any two correct sketches differ by a **vertical shift**: the derivative only records
    slopes, and sliding a graph up or down changes no slope.
4.  If $f$ is one such function, the others are exactly the functions $f + C$, $C$ a constant.
    That every function with the same derivative arises this way is a real theorem, not just a
    picture: it says that a function with derivative $0$ on an interval is constant, which
    follows from the mean value theorem (C&J §2.8.h, §2.9.b). The graph of $f'$ determines
    $f$ only up to this one unknown number.
5.  The condition $f(-2) = -1$ pins down the constant: of all the vertical shifts, exactly one
    passes through the point $(-2,-1)$. The red graph is the unique answer, with
    $f(-4)=1$, $f(0)=1$, $f(2)=5$, $f(3)=6$, $f(4)=5$. (Explicitly: $f(x)=\tfrac12x^2+2x+1$ on
    $[-4,0]$, $f(x)=2x+1$ on $[0,2]$, $f(x)=-x^2+6x-3$ on $[2,4]$.)
:::

### Problem 4

Here $f$ is continuous on $[-3,3]$ and differentiable everywhere except at $x=0$; its derivative
is shown below.

```{python}
#| label: fig-deriv-p4
#| fig-cap: "Problem 4: the graph of $f'$ (top) and two sets of axes for your sketches of $f$. The open circles indicate that $f'(0)$ is undefined."
#| echo: false
fig, (ax_d, ax_a, ax_b) = stacked((-3, 3), [((-2, 4), "Graph of $f'$", "$y$"),
                                             ((-3, 3), "Axes A: sketches for part 2", "$y$"),
                                             ((-3, 3), "Axes B: sketch for part 3", "$y$")])
curve(ax_d, f4p_left, -3, 0); curve(ax_d, f4p_right, 0, 3)
hole(ax_d, 0, 1); hole(ax_d, 0, 3)
plt.show()
```

::: {#exr-deriv-p4}
1.  Read off the main features of $f$. In particular: what kind of point is $x=-1$? What does the
    graph of $f$ look like at $x=0$? Does $f$ have a maximum or minimum at $x=2$?
2.  On axes A, sketch two different functions with the derivative shown.
3.  Now you are told that
    $$
    f(2) = 1.
    $$
    Sketch $f$ on axes B. Read off approximate values of $f(-3)$, $f(-1)$, $f(0)$, and $f(3)$.
:::

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| label: fig-deriv-p4-sol
#| fig-cap: "Solution to Problem 4. Gray: several functions with the given derivative. Red: the one with $f(2) = 1$."
#| echo: false
fig, (ax_d, ax_s) = stacked((-3, 3), [((-2, 4), "$f'$", "$y$"), ((-3, 3), "$f$", "$y$")])
curve(ax_d, f4p_left, -3, 0); curve(ax_d, f4p_right, 0, 3)
hole(ax_d, 0, 1); hole(ax_d, 0, 3)
for c in (-2.5, -2, 0, 0.5):
    curve(ax_s, lambda x, c=c: f4(x, c), -3, 3, color=GRAY, lw=1.3)
curve(ax_s, lambda x: f4(x, -1), -3, 3, color=RED)
dot(ax_s, 2, 1)
guides((ax_d, ax_s), (-1, 0, 2))
plt.show()
```

1.  $f'$ changes sign from $-$ to $+$ at $x=-1$: a local minimum. At $x=0$ the slope jumps from
    $1$ to $3$: $f$ has a **corner** there (the reverse of Problem 2). At $x=2$, $f'$ touches
    zero without changing sign: $f$ has a horizontal tangent but keeps increasing — no extremum.
    $f$ bends up on $[-3,0]$ and on $[2,3]$, and bends down on $[0,2]$.
2.  Again, any two answers differ by a vertical shift.
3.  Only one shift passes through $(2,1)$: $f(-3)=0.5$, $f(-1)=-1.5$, $f(0)=-1$, $f(3)=1.25$.
    To reach the left half from the given point you must pass *through* the corner, and this is
    where the continuity of $f$ at $0$ is used (see Going Further, question 3).
:::

## Going further

::: {#exr-deriv-further}
1.  **Change as area.** In Problem 3, compute the signed area between the graph of $f'$ and the
    $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=3$ (it is made of triangles and a rectangle). Compare it with
    $f(3) - f(-2)$ from your sketch. Repeat for another pair of points. What do you conjecture?
2.  **Why the real numbers matter.** Define $h$ on the *rational* numbers by $h(x) = 0$ if
    $x < \sqrt2$ and $h(x) = 1$ if $x > \sqrt2$. Convince yourself that at every rational $x$,
    the graph of $h$ is flat nearby, so its "derivative" is $0$ everywhere on $\Q$. Yet $h$ is not
    constant. Which property of $\R$ (from the first weeks of the course) rules this out for
    functions on a real interval?
3.  **Is one value always enough?** In Problem 4, drop the assumption that $f$ is continuous at
    $0$, so $f$ is only required to have the given derivative on $[-3,0)$ and on $(0,3]$. Does
    $f(2) = 1$ still determine $f$? How many function values would you need?
:::

::: {.solution}
1.  The area is $2$ (triangle on $[-2,0]$) $+\ 4$ (rectangle on $[0,2]$) $+\ 1$ (triangle on
    $[2,3]$) $= 7$, and indeed $f(3) - f(-2) = 6 - (-1) = 7$. The conjecture
    $$
    f(b) - f(a) = \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx
    $$
    is the **fundamental theorem of calculus** (C&J §2.9). It explains the ambiguity in a second
    way: $f'$ determines every *difference* $f(b)-f(a)$, but not the starting height.
2.  On $\Q$ the jump of $h$ happens across a "hole" at $\sqrt2$ that contains no input of $h$.
    On $\R$ there are no such holes: this is completeness (the nested interval principle). The
    proof that $f'=0$ forces $f$ constant goes through the mean value theorem, which in turn
    rests on completeness.
3.  No. On each of the two pieces $f$ is determined up to its own constant, and without
    continuity the two constants are independent: the left half of the graph can be shifted
    up or down on its own. You need one value from each side of $0$ — for instance $f(2)$ and
    $f(-1)$. The principle is: one value per *interval* on which $f$ is differentiable.
:::
